newsitem.title: UK: Gold Outlook - Market seen lacking will to rally.
newsitem.headline: Gold Outlook - Market seen lacking will to rally.

text.p: The gold market fell to its lowest level in over four years on Friday afternoon, and dealers saw little to suggest any will to rally this week after further weakness early on Monday.
The price was under pressure all last week and a boost for the dollar on Friday following the release of the best U.S. gross dometic product data in a decade was the last straw for gold.
A 50-point surge in the Dow Jones Industrial average did not help the metal either as speculative money flooded into U.S. equities and foreign exchange.
Gold's lowest fix since April 1 1993 came in at $336.55 an ounce, 35 cents under the previous four-year low set on February 12.
"It had been well supported by physical buying at $337.00 before that, but the professionals decided to give at a go on Friday morning and the firmer dollar did the rest," a dealer said.

That had completed a gloomy week for gold in which the market slipped below the long standing support at $340.00 on Tuesday and never looked like seriously challenging that level for the rest of the week.
A report from SBC Warburg sounded alarms on Thursday when it announced a downgrading of its gold price forecasts through to the end of the century.

The average prices for 1998 and 1999 where reduced by 9.5 percent and 13 percent respectively to $335 per ounce for both years (from $370 and $385) and the 1997 average was cut to $345.00 from $352.00.
SBC Warburg's global head of commodity research Peter Richardson said, "This is a conservative outlook. We are basically saying to investors, 'be very cautious'."

The report said of the medium term outlook, "This extended period of low prices is designed to reflect our concerns about a number of key issues that are expected to dominate the gold market over the next two and a half years."
Key factors involved were the absence of investment buying anticipated in a future of moderate sustainable growth and low inflation.
There was also the continuing threat of official sales and lending from central banks and other institutions like the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
But also significant was continued forward selling by producers and the likelihood that mine supply would be cut only marginally at the forecast price levels.
An estimated 753 tonnes of additional gold would be delivered to the market through hedging by new and existing mines protecting themselves against low prices during the period.

The increase was likely due to new management and ownership in the South African industry possibly triggering new or increased hedging programmes, fresh hedging from North American producers which had unwound earlier positions and new mines being obliged to hedge by the terms of their project financing agreements.
"Investors can't look for salvation from the supply and demand fundamentals in gold mining as they can in other industries," said Richardson.
He estimated that at the report's forecast prices, only a net 32 tonnes of mine production would be cut due to unprofitability in 1999.
"Obviously if the price turns out to be lower, then there will be larger losses of production," Richardson said.
However the estimated mine cutback would be more than offset by higher sales from central banks.
SBC Warburg estimated net official sales at 250 tonnes this year, 263 tonnes in 1998 and 276 tonnes in 1999.
The market's short term prospects hinged increasingly on the old market adage that when everybody was convinced a price is going to fall, it wopuld often do the opposite.
"Gold could be a classic case of a price reaching its bottom. Nobody wants it and everybody is bearish so that is the time to buy," one dealer said.

Rhona O'Connell, metals markets analyst at stockbroker T. Hoare and Co, held the same view but added that the very calm inflationary and financial environment in which gold was slumping would have to change before a recovery was sustainable.

"It needs short covering but that will only happen on changed external parameters," she said, ading that at such low prices the gold miners might be unwilling to sell into the market to lock in their profit margins.
--Brian Spoors London Newsroom +44 171 542 8058
